prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: From, Mithridatic, Wars

outputs.L1:
From the Mithridatic Wars, first century BC

Our general was elsewhere, but we drowned.  
While he rested, he sent us home  
with the greater part of his spoils,  
the weight that had burdened his army.

The thrashing storm that found us  
split the hulls  
and made of us offerings to the seabed—  
a rain of statues, gold, and men.

Released from service,  
finished with war,  
the crash and hiss grown silent,  
we fell through streams of creatures  
whose lives were purpose enough.

We settled among treasure looted  
from the ruined temples of Athenian Greece;  
among us, bronze and marble gods and goddesses  
lay moored without grace,  
avoided by incurious fish.

Their power was never meant to keep us afloat—  
our pleasures were incidental gifts—  
but, shaken by their radiance in our dust,  
we had given them our voices.

Their faces, wings, and limbs  
lie here with our sanded bones  
and motionless devices.

Small crabs try to wear rings  
set with agate and amethyst,  
and many an octopus,  
seeking an hour’s rest,  
finds shelter in our brain-cases.

So we remain of use.
outputs.L2:
From the Mithridatic Wars, in the first century BC:

Our commander was not with us,  
yet we were the ones who sank.

As he took his ease,  
he sent us back across the water  
with most of the plunder  
that had burdened his troops.

The violent storm that overtook us  
split the ships’ hulls open  
and delivered us to the bottom of the sea:  
statues, gold, and human bodies  
falling like rain.

Freed from duty,  
finished with battle,  
the wreck’s roar and seething quieted,  
we descended through currents alive with creatures  
whose existence needed no further reason.

We came to rest beside treasure stolen  
from the shattered temples of Athenian Greece.  
Around us, bronze and marble deities—  
gods and goddesses—  
were anchored clumsily,  
ignored by fish that swam around them.

Their divinity had never been intended  
to keep us afloat.  
Any comfort we took from them  
was accidental.  
Still, awed by their brightness  
amid our ruin,  
we had lent them our voices.

Their faces, wings, and limbs  
remain here now  
with our polished bones  
and our unmoving instruments.

Small crabs try to wear rings  
mounted with agate and amethyst,  
and many an octopus,  
wanting a brief place to rest,  
takes refuge inside our skulls.

So even now,  
we serve some purpose.
outputs.L3:
The speaker and his fellow soldiers drowned at sea while being shipped home with the spoils taken during the Mithridatic Wars. After surviving war and plunder, they were loaded onto vessels along with the wealth they had seized: statues, gold, sacred objects, and other treasures stripped from temples and cities in Greece, including ruined Athens.

During the voyage, a violent storm struck the fleet. The ships were broken apart by the force of the wind and waves, and everything they carried was cast into the sea. Men, weapons, statues of gods, precious metals, and temple offerings all sank together to the ocean floor. The soldiers who had helped carry off these riches came to rest beside the very objects they had looted.

In death, they lay among sacred things that had once inspired awe and reverence. The images of gods, the treasures of temples, and the symbols of human power and devotion were now powerless beneath the water. No worshippers approached them, no priests tended them, and no armies fought to possess them. The divine statues and the soldiers’ bones were reduced to the same silence, lying together in the deep.

Over time, the sea transformed these remains. What had once been honored as sacred, valued as wealth, or feared as military strength became part of an underwater world. Sea creatures moved through the wreckage, made homes in the hollow spaces, and used bones, armor, and treasures as shelter. In this way, the drowned soldiers and their stolen riches found a new purpose beneath the waves, no longer as objects of conquest or worship, but as part of the life of the sea.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a haunting meditation on soldiers who drown while transporting spoils taken during the Mithridatic Wars. Speaking in a first-person collective voice, the dead soldiers recall their final journey not as a triumphal return but as a slow descent beneath the sea. They sink together with the cargo of conquest: looted statues, sacred objects, treasure, weapons, and the bodies of the defeated and the victors alike. The “we” of the poem gives the drowned men a shared identity, making them less like individual heroes than remnants of a vast imperial machine. Their voices seem to rise from underwater, where memory, history, and physical decay merge.

Much of the poem’s power comes from its underwater imagery. The sea transforms everything it receives. Gold, marble, armor, and human flesh are all carried downward and stripped of the meanings they once had on land. Objects that once signified empire, religion, wealth, and victory become part of the ocean floor. Statues that may have been worshipped as sacred images or admired as trophies are no longer elevated on pedestals; they lie among silt, weeds, shells, and bones. Treasure that once inspired violence and ambition is rendered useless in the depths. The soldiers’ own bodies, formerly instruments of war, become indistinguishable from the wreckage around them.

In this way, the poem undermines the idea of imperial glory. The spoils of war are not shown in a parade or placed in a temple; instead, they are scattered beneath the waves. What had been seized in the name of power, victory, or devotion is reduced to seabed debris. Marine life reclaims the remains of conquest: fish swim through helmets and broken vessels, plants cling to statues, and creatures make homes among the ruins. Nature does not honor the categories that humans create. It does not distinguish between sacred and profane, conqueror and conquered, treasure and trash. Everything becomes material to be absorbed, covered, and reused.

The poem also questions the relationship between violence and faith. The plundered religious objects suggest that sacred things have been drawn into the brutal logic of empire. What was once revered becomes cargo; what was once protected becomes loot. Yet the sea’s transformation of these objects suggests that human claims to holiness and possession are fragile. In the ocean, the gods, their images, and their worshippers all suffer the same fate. The poem does not necessarily deny the sacred, but it shows how easily human beings corrupt it through conquest and greed.

Ultimately, the poem offers a vision of historical humility. The soldiers may have believed they were serving a great cause, enriching an empire, or participating in an immortal victory. But their end is anonymous and material. They do not become legends; they become part of the ocean’s hidden landscape. The poem suggests that human ambition, however grand, is temporary. Empires rise, armies march, treasures are stolen, and temples are emptied, but nature outlasts them all. Beneath the sea, the trophies of war lose their splendor, and the violence that produced them is silenced. What remains is not glory, but wreckage—absorbed into a world indifferent to human pride.
outputs.L5:
The Mithridatic Wars were a series of three major conflicts fought between the Roman Republic and Mithridates VI, the powerful king of Pontus, from 88 BCE to 63 BCE. These wars were among the most important struggles for control of the eastern Mediterranean.

Mithridates VI, often called Mithridates the Great, sought to expand his influence across Asia Minor and challenge Roman power. He gained support from many cities that resented Roman taxation and rule. The First Mithridatic War began after Mithridates ordered the massacre of thousands of Romans and Italians in Asia Minor, an event known as the Asiatic Vespers. Rome responded by sending the general Sulla, who defeated Mithridates and forced him to accept peace.

The Second Mithridatic War was shorter and less decisive, but tensions remained high. The Third Mithridatic War became the longest and most significant. Roman generals Lucullus and later Pompey led campaigns against Mithridates, gradually weakening his kingdom. Pompey finally defeated him, and Mithridates fled to the Bosporan Kingdom, where he later died.

From the Mithridatic Wars, Rome gained greater control over Asia Minor and the eastern Mediterranean. These conflicts also increased the fame and power of Roman generals, especially Pompey. The wars marked a major step in Rome’s transformation from an Italian power into a dominant empire across the Mediterranean world.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the collective voice of Roman soldiers drowned in a shipwreck during the Mithridatic Wars, surrounded on the sea floor by looted Greek temple treasures and statues.
counterfactuals.output:
We went down still wearing the empire.

Iron at the ribs,  
bronze at the mouth,  
salt entering us like a second oath.

Above, the storm tore our orders into gulls.  
The captain shouted Rome,  
the oars shouted home,  
the sea answered in the old language  
no consul ever mastered.

Now we are a legion of drowned men  
counted by crabs,  
mustered by moonlight that cannot reach us entire.

Around us: the gods we stole.

Apollo lies on his side in the silt,  
one marble eye filled with sand,  
his fingers broken from the lyre  
as if music were a thing that could be packed in straw  
and carried west.

Athena, green with weed,  
keeps her helmet on.  
We never saw her look so patient.  
At Delos, at Chios, at Pergamon,  
we called it tribute,  
spoils,  
the due of victory—  
now her bronze hand hovers above us  
not in blessing,  
not in blame,  
but in the perfect stillness of someone  
who has outlived every excuse.

Gold cups bloom with anemones.  
Tripods cradle eels.  
Coins spill from amphorae  
like little suns we cannot spend.  
A temple door, pried loose by axes,  
rests against the hull  
as though the sea itself  
has built a shrine from our theft.

We remember the harbors—  
pitch smoke, mule sweat, wine,  
the Greek boys watching us load their ancestors  
into our black-bellied ship.

We laughed then.  
We had names then.

Lucius with the scar through his lip.  
Marcus who carved his daughter’s initials  
inside his shield.  
Aulus, who feared deep water  
and crossed himself to every god,  
ours or theirs,  
before boarding.

Now our names loosen.  
They leave us in bubbles.  
They rise faster than prayers.

Mithridates still burns somewhere in the mouths of men.  
Senators still argue under painted ceilings.  
Generals still unfold maps  
and press their rings into wax.  
But here, beneath the green weight,  
kingdoms are only sediment.

We lie with our plunder  
and learn its silence.

The statues do not sink lower.  
They do not rot.  
Their calm becomes the weather of this place.  
We, who marched beneath eagles,  
are softened, opened,  
taken joint by joint  
into the republic of fish.

O mothers of Italy,  
do not wait at the road.

O wives, take new husbands.  
O sons, inherit nothing from us  
but the warning of iron.

We were told the world was a road  
and Rome its end.  
We found instead  
a floor of broken offerings,  
a dark field where helmets fill with sand,  
where the sea  
with infinite small hands  
returns every stolen god  
to worship.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary ekphrastic poem about the Antikythera shipwreck, narrated by the dead crew and cargo, mentioning statues, gold, gods, fish, crabs, octopuses, and the Antikythera mechanism without naming it directly.
counterfactuals.output:
We sank with our mouths full of thunder,  
with amphorae knocking like knees in the dark,  
with statues turning their marble faces  
toward the last blue coin of sky.

We were the crew, salt-blinded, rope-burned,  
calling to gods who had already gone  
to sleep in their temples of cloud.  
We were the cargo too: bronze shoulders,  
gold hidden in the ship’s ribs,  
wine sealed in clay, a philosopher’s hand  
broken from its argument.

Down we went, past the reach of oars,  
past gull-cry, sail-snap, market, empire,  
into the green court of fish.  
They inspected our open eyes,  
our sandals, our teeth,  
the delicate machinery of our bones.

Crabs became our stewards.  
They filed through the treasure chests,  
clicked over coins,  
tasted the kings stamped there  
and found them no sweeter than stone.  
Octopuses, those soft-bodied priests,  
entered the hollow statues  
and wore the gods from within.

O Apollo, whose bronze hair darkened,  
O Herakles, muscle furred with weed,  
O Aphrodite, beautiful in her damage—  
you learned the patience of wreckage.  
Your plinths dissolved.  
Your names loosened.  
Your temples became coral.

And among us lay a small corroded oracle,  
green with centuries,  
its wheels nested like moons in a drowned skull.  
It had once taught bronze to think  
of eclipses, seasons, wandering stars;  
had turned the heavens by hand  
for men who could not turn away from fate.

Now it kept a slower calendar:  
the molt of crabs,  
the bloom of sponge,  
the silver grammar of fish,  
the octopus folding night  
into its eight secret sleeves.

We speak from under Antikythera,  
from the hush below the storm’s memory.  
We are sailors and statues, gold and gods,  
cargo and corpse, all inventoried by sand.  
Above us, history raises its lamp;  
below, the sea keeps counting—  
tooth by tooth, gear by gear,  
star by drowned star.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a haunting historical poem set in the first century BC: Sulla has sent home plunder from Athens, the ship sinks in a storm, and the drowned men reflect on becoming useful to sea creatures.
counterfactuals.output:
**After Sulla’s Cargo**

When Sulla stripped Athena’s wounded hill,  
the bronze gods stared with rain in their eyes.  
Books, cups, bright tripods, votive gold—  
all crated in the reek of conquest—  
were lowered to the Roman holds.

We were the hands beneath the ropes,  
the backs beneath another city’s grief.  
We laughed, perhaps. Men laugh  
when they are tired,  
when temples fall,  
when no god answers from the smoke.

Then westward: wine-dark, iron-dark,  
the sea rose up as if it knew  
what weight we carried.  
The mast cracked like a verdict.  
Lightning opened the clouds  
and found us guilty.

Athens sank again that night—  
not marble, not memory,  
but shields and bowls and statues’ severed hands  
turning slowly downward,  
each treasure learning  
the cold grammar of the deep.

We followed.

At first we clawed for Rome,  
for wives with lamps, for children’s hair,  
for the sour bread of morning.  
But the storm took language from our mouths  
and packed it neatly in our lungs.

Now we lie where no triumph passes.  
No laurel rots above us.  
No senator names our service.  
The eels have entered our sleeves  
like slender household gods.  
Small fish shelter in the cage of ribs.  
Coral, patient as an old historian,  
writes red letters on our bones.

We are useful at last.

A crab wears my finger-joint  
as Sulla wore a ring.  
My skull, rinsed clean of orders,  
keeps a blenny from the current.  
My brother’s teeth, once clenched  
against the lash and oar,  
are white stones for an octopus’s door.

O Athens, forgive us if you can.  
Your stolen silver feeds the dark.  
Your sacred bronze grows furred with weed.  
The owl of wisdom, drowned in green,  
looks out from under anemones  
with eyes that do not close.

And we, who bore away your glory,  
bear now the eggs of cuttlefish,  
the sleep of worms,  
the slow republic of the sand.

Above, men will say the sea was cruel.  
They will rebuild the ledgers,  
curse the loss,  
send divers, prayers, another fleet.

But here below the storm is over.  
Here conquest loosens its fist.  
Here every empire is softened,  
opened,  
made hollow enough for life.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose-poem from the perspective of drowned ancient sailors lying with bronze and marble sculptures on the ocean floor after a Roman war, blending archaeology, mythology, and marine life.
counterfactuals.output:
We have forgotten the name of the battle, though iron remembers. It blooms red in the sand beside us, nail and spearhead and the bitten rims of shields, while the sea combs everything slowly into relic. Once, above, there were orders shouted in Latin, oars striking time, the high bronze throat of a trumpet, the bright terrible weather of fire. Now there is only the long blue silence, and our ribs are amphorae the eels enter and leave without ceremony.

We lie among gods who also fell.

A marble Apollo rests on his side, cheek pressed to the silt, his broken hand extended as if still asking the waves for a lyre. A bronze athlete, green with centuries, runs nowhere; barnacles have given him a second skin, and a small octopus nests in the hollow behind his knee. Aphrodite’s face, cracked at the mouth, receives the kisses of anemones. The sea has dressed emperors and slaves alike in the same soft robe of algae.

Do not pity us. We have become part of a country older than Rome.

Above us, divers descend like hesitant souls, trailing their silver bubbles toward the sun. They touch nothing at first. Their lamps move over us as moons move over ruins. They point to the cargo, to the marble torsos, to the stamped ingots, to the blackened timbers of the galley pinned beneath sand. They will give the wreck a number, draw its bones on waterproof tablets, lift a cup, a coin, a god’s shoulder. They will say: second century before the common era, perhaps; evidence of trade, of plunder, of imperial appetite; a ship lost after conflict, carrying spoils or tribute.

They will not know how Lucius sang when afraid. They will not know that Menon of Rhodes kept a fig in his pouch for luck, or that the boy with the split lip had never seen Rome and believed Neptune lived in every green wave, large enough to swallow fleets and merciful enough to return a mother’s prayer. They will not know that, as we sank, the statues seemed to rise.

O Poseidon, Ennosigaios, Earth-Shaker, horse-lord of the foam—were we payment? Did you count us like coins into your palm? Or was it Mars who spent us, flinging our names into the water after the broken mast? We have had centuries to argue with gods. The gods do not answer. Marble answers more faithfully: it keeps the curve of a thigh, the fold of a cloak, the calm of a face carved before disaster learned its language.

Fish pass through the senate of our bones. Parrotfish graze the old paint from a goddess’s hair. Sea fans write red petitions in the current. A moray opens and closes its jaws in the helmet of a centurion, speaking the only prophecy left: salt, salt, salt. At night, when the moon lays its ladder on the surface, bioluminescence gathers around us, and we seem again to wear stars on our tunics, to carry lanterns through the streets of some submerged Ostia where no tax is levied, no chain tightened, no banner raised.

We are the drowned, yes, but also the keepers. We hold the last position of the ship. We cradle the cargo Rome desired and the sea accepted. We are catalog and caution, offering and witness. Let the scholars brush sand from the inscription; let them argue over provenance, quarry, alloy, school. Let them lift Apollo into air and marvel at the green fire of bronze returned from darkness.

But leave some part of us here.

Leave us the anchor stone, the snapped oar, the little cup turned upward like a begging hand. Leave us the company of cuttlefish, the slow applause of weeds, the marble gods who learned at last to be humble. Leave us beneath the pressure and the blue, where war has no trumpet, where empire comes down to a shard, where every conquering hand is opened by water.

We sleep, and do not sleep. We erode into legend. We listen as the sea rehearses our names, never correctly, never the same way twice, until even error becomes music.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an elegiac poem titled or beginning “From the Mithridatic Wars, first century BC,” in which dead soldiers describe sinking with looted treasure and ending as shelter for octopuses and crabs.
counterfactuals.output:
**From the Mithridatic Wars, first century BC,**

we went down slowly, still in our armor,  
the sea accepting us without triumph.  
Above, the gulls cried over broken oars;  
below, the bronze coins loosened from our belts  
and turned like little moons into the dark.

We had taken cups from temples,  
rings from the hands of men who prayed,  
purple cloth, small gods with silver eyes.  
All night the ship groaned under our plunder,  
as if wealth itself were ballast enough  
to pull a kingdom under.

We remember the last light—  
a red seam over Pontus,  
Mithridates’ name shouted through smoke,  
Rome’s eagles black against the burning sails.  
Then water entered every wound.  
Then silence learned our language.

Now the gold lies green beside our ribs.  
Amphorae lean like tired sentries in the sand.  
Our helmets, once bright with fear,  
are houses for the shy and many-armed.  
Octopuses flower through our eyeholes,  
soft kings of the ruin we became.

Crabs come sidling over our breastplates,  
tapping the old medals of bone,  
and sleep beneath the shields  
we lifted against spears and weather.  
No captain calls us to order.  
No mother hears which wave took whom.

Only the tide counts us,  
returning and returning,  
touching each coin, each tooth, each blade  
with the same cold mercy.  
What we stole has outlasted the hands that stole it.  
What we were has opened into shelter.

O land of dust and laurel, keep your victories.  
We have gone where banners cannot follow.  
In the blue dusk under the keel’s shadow,  
we give our hollow chests to the living:  
to crab, to weed, to watchful octopus—  
and are, at last, forgiven by the sea.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
